title: NIST SP 800-53B
subtitle: Control baselines, categorisation and tailoring
source: NIST SP 800-53B (Oct 2020, updated Dec 2020), FIPS 199/200, SP 800-37 Rev. 2; baseline allocations from NIST OSCAL profiles for Release 5.2.0
description: How to pick and tailor controls: FIPS 199 categorisation and the high-water mark, the Low, Moderate, High and Privacy baselines, the six tailoring actions, overlays, full allocation tables by family and a worked case.

chapters.title: About SP 800-53B
chapters.summary: What the baselines are, how they relate to SP 800-53, and how big each one is.

blocks.text: **NIST SP 800-53B**, *Control Baselines for Information Systems and Organizations* (October 2020, updated December 2020), turns the SP 800-53 catalog into ready-made starting points. A **control baseline** is a predefined set of controls and enhancements that addresses the protection needs of a group of systems or organisations.

rows: System processes personally identifiable information, whatever its impact level

items: The three **security baselines** are cumulative in practice: High contains everything in Moderate, which contains everything in Low.
They draw from **18 of the 20 families**. PM (organisation-level) and PT (privacy) are not in the security baselines.
The **privacy baseline** draws from 16 families and is applied in addition to a security baseline when the system processes PII.
Release 5.2.0 added new controls to the catalog but **did not add them to any baseline**.

blocks.title: One catalog, many baselines
blocks.text: SP 800-53 = everything available. SP 800-53B = NIST's recommended starting selection. Your tailored baseline = what your system actually implements.

rows: Impact level for confidentiality, integrity, availability
Controls built and described in the SSP

blocks.title: The key link
blocks.text: The baseline you start from is decided by the system's categorisation. RA-2 (security categorisation), PL-10 (baseline selection) and PL-11 (baseline tailoring) are the catalog controls that require this process.

rows: Personally Identifiable Information Processing and Transparency

blocks.title: Reading the table
blocks.text: AC has many more items at High than at Low because access control enhancements (automation, stronger separation, session controls) are added as impact rises. PT appears only in the Privacy column.

quiz.q: What is a control baseline?
options: A predefined set of controls addressing protection needs of a group of systems
quiz.explain: Baselines are starting sets of controls.

quiz.q: How many items are in the Moderate baseline (Release 5.2.0)?
quiz.explain: Low 149, Moderate 287, High 370, Privacy 96.

quiz.q: When is the privacy baseline applied?
options: When the system processes PII, whatever its impact level
quiz.explain: The privacy baseline depends on PII processing, not on impact level.

quiz.q: Which families are not in the security baselines?
quiz.explain: PM is organisation-level; PT is privacy.

quiz.q: Were the new Release 5.2.0 controls added to the baselines?
quiz.explain: SA-24, SA-15(13) and SI-2(7) were not allocated to baselines.

chapters.title: Security categorisation (FIPS 199)
chapters.summary: Impact levels, security categories, the high-water mark and how categorisation picks the baseline.

blocks.text: FIPS 199 defines three levels of potential impact on organisations or individuals if confidentiality, integrity or availability is lost:

rows: Minor degradation of mission capability; minor damage to assets; minor financial loss; minor harm to individuals
Significant degradation of mission; significant damage to assets; significant financial loss; significant harm to individuals (not loss of life)
Severe degradation or loss of mission; major damage to assets; major financial loss; severe or catastrophic harm, including loss of life or serious life-threatening injury

blocks.text: Categorisation is done per **information type** (e.g. payroll data, public web content, patient records), rating confidentiality, integrity and availability separately. **SP 800-60** suggests provisional impact levels for common information types.
The notation is: **SC** information type = {(confidentiality, impact), (integrity, impact), (availability, impact)}. Confidentiality of public information can be NA.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: Customer account data: SC = {(confidentiality, MODERATE), (integrity, MODERATE), (availability, LOW)}. Public product brochure: SC = {(confidentiality, NA), (integrity, LOW), (availability, LOW)}.

A system usually processes several information types. The system's category takes the **highest impact** for each objective across all its information types. Under FIPS 200, the **overall impact level** of the system is the highest value among confidentiality, integrity and availability, and that level selects the Low, Moderate or High baseline.

Overall impact level: **High**, so the HR and payroll system starts from the High baseline, even though only integrity reached High. Tailoring can then address this, for example by focusing extra integrity controls where they matter.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Categorising the system by its most important function rather than all information types; rating everything High "to be safe" (expensive and unfocused); forgetting availability for systems the business can't run without.

US national security systems use **CNSSI 1253**, which does not apply a single high-water mark. It keeps separate impact values for confidentiality, integrity and availability (e.g. Moderate-High-Low) and selects controls accordingly, then applies CNSS overlays.

quiz.q: Under FIPS 199, a 'serious' adverse effect corresponds to which impact level?
quiz.explain: Limited = Low, serious = Moderate, severe or catastrophic = High.

quiz.q: A system's C/I/A values are Low, Moderate, Low. Which baseline applies under the high-water mark?
quiz.explain: The highest value (Moderate) sets the overall impact level.

quiz.q: Which publication suggests provisional impact levels for information types?
quiz.explain: SP 800-60 maps information types to impact levels.

quiz.q: Which approach keeps separate C, I and A values rather than one overall level?
quiz.explain: CNSSI 1253 for national security systems.

quiz.q: Why is rating every system High a poor practice?
options: It drives unnecessary cost and dilutes focus on real risks
quiz.explain: Controls should be proportionate to impact.

chapters.title: Selecting controls
chapters.summary: Baseline and organisation-generated approaches, the privacy baseline, and the assumptions behind the baselines.

rows: Start from the Low, Moderate or High baseline (plus Privacy if PII), then tailor
Most systems; consistent, efficient, expected by US federal authorisers
Build the control set bottom-up from requirements, risk assessment and threat analysis, using the catalog
Unique systems (e.g. specialised OT, weapons, IoT) where baselines fit poorly

blocks.text: Both approaches end in the same place: a documented, justified set of controls in the system security plan. Many organisations combine them: start from a baseline and supplement with controls identified by risk assessment.

items: Selected when the system processes PII, as determined with the senior agency official for privacy (or equivalent).
Not tied to FIPS 199 impact levels: a low-impact system that processes PII still needs the privacy baseline.
Includes privacy-focused controls such as PT-2 to PT-8, RA-8 (privacy impact assessments), SI-18 and SI-19, plus privacy-relevant parts of many families and organisation-level PM controls.
Privacy officials and security officials collaborate on controls that serve both (joint controls).

blocks.text: NIST built the baselines around a typical system: one that sits in physical facilities, holds persistent user data, serves multiple users, connects to other systems and uses common commercial technology. The more your system differs, the more tailoring you should expect.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A standalone, air-gapped laboratory instrument doesn't need most remote access (AC-17) or boundary protection (SC-7) requirements designed for networked systems. Scoping them out, with written rationale, is legitimate tailoring.

Many catalog items are in no baseline. They are not less important; they address specific threats, technologies or high-assurance needs, and are added through tailoring or overlays. Examples: SC-26 decoys, RA-10 threat hunting, SI-20 tainting, SA-24 design for cyber resiliency.

quiz.q: Which selection approach builds the control set from requirements and risk without starting from a baseline?
quiz.explain: Organisation-generated selection is bottom-up.

quiz.q: A low-impact system processes customer names and emails. What applies?
options: Low baseline plus the privacy baseline
quiz.explain: PII triggers the privacy baseline regardless of impact level.

quiz.q: Why might an air-gapped lab instrument remove AC-17 during tailoring?
options: It has no remote access, so the control doesn't apply
quiz.explain: Scoping considerations remove inapplicable controls, with rationale.

quiz.q: Controls not in any baseline are...
options: Available for tailoring and overlays when threats or needs justify them
quiz.explain: They are added when needed.

chapters.title: Tailoring
chapters.summary: The six tailoring actions, scoping, compensating controls, parameters, supplementing and documentation.

items: **Identify and designate common controls** that the system inherits (e.g. data centre physical security, enterprise IAM).
**Apply scoping considerations** to decide which remaining controls apply and where.
**Select compensating controls** where a baseline control can't be implemented.
**Assign values to organisation-defined parameters** in assignment and selection statements.
**Supplement the baseline** with additional controls or enhancements where risk requires.
**Provide specification information** for implementation (e.g. how a mechanism must be configured).

blocks.title: Tailoring is expected
blocks.text: NIST designed baselines as starting points. Tailoring, with documented rationale, is part of the RMF Select step (Task S-2 in SP 800-37), not a way around it.
Typical considerations that change whether or where a control applies:

rows: Boundary protection applies at the network edge component, not on every workstation
A system in a guarded facility may scope physical controls differently from one at a remote site
Controls for wireless (AC-18) don't apply if the system has no wireless capability
Cloud-hosted systems inherit most PE controls from the provider
Identification controls for public read-only websites differ from internal systems
Availability controls may be stronger for systems supporting critical services

items: Used when a baseline control can't be implemented, or isn't cost-effective, and an alternative gives equivalent or comparable protection.
Prefer controls from the SP 800-53 catalog; document why the original can't be used and how the alternative addresses the same risk.
The risk owner or authorising official accepts any remaining risk.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: A legacy medical device can't support account lockout (AC-7). Compensating controls: network isolation on a dedicated VLAN, access only through a jump host that enforces lockout and MFA, and enhanced monitoring of the device's logs.

rows: Consecutive invalid logon attempts and time period
SP 800-63B aligned; MFA for all access
Vulnerability scanning frequency and remediation times
Monthly scans; critical fixed in 15 days
Critical within 15 days, high within 30 days

blocks.title: Values must be justified
blocks.text: Choose values from risk, regulation and capability. FedRAMP and other programmes define many values for you; outside those, record the rationale in the SSP.

items: **Supplement** when the risk assessment, threat intelligence or requirements show gaps, e.g. adding RA-10 threat hunting or SC-26 decoys for a high-value asset.
**Document** every tailoring decision in the system security plan: what was added, removed, compensated or parameterised, and why.
**Level of detail** scales with risk: decisions for high-impact systems and high-value assets need more justification than for low-impact systems.
**Review** tailoring when the system, threats or requirements change.

quiz.q: Which is one of the six tailoring actions?
quiz.explain: The others are not tailoring actions.

quiz.q: A system can't implement AC-7 lockout. What is the right tailoring response?
options: Select a documented compensating control that gives comparable protection
quiz.explain: Compensating controls with rationale and risk acceptance.

quiz.q: Where are tailoring decisions documented?
quiz.explain: The SSP records the tailored baseline and rationale.

quiz.q: Which scoping consideration explains a cloud SaaS system inheriting PE controls?
quiz.explain: Physical infrastructure is the provider's.

quiz.q: When should you supplement a baseline?
options: When the risk assessment or requirements show the baseline is insufficient
quiz.explain: Supplementing addresses risk-specific gaps.

chapters.title: Overlays
chapters.summary: What overlays are, examples, and how they combine with baselines.

blocks.text: An **overlay** is a fully specified set of tailoring decisions (controls added or removed, parameter values, extra guidance) for a community of interest, technology or environment. It is applied on top of a baseline, so many organisations can reuse the same tailoring.

items: **Communities:** e.g. healthcare, financial services, intelligence.
**Technologies:** e.g. cloud, mobile, industrial control systems, cross-domain solutions, AI.
**Environments or information types:** e.g. classified information, privacy, space systems.

rows: CNSSI 1253 overlays (e.g. Privacy, Classified Information, Space Platform, Cross Domain Solution)
Tailoring for US national security systems
Tailors Low, Moderate and High baselines for operational technology and industrial control systems
Tailored SP 800-53 Rev. 5 baselines with parameter values for cloud services used by US agencies
NIST Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems (COSAIS)
NIST project to develop SP 800-53 overlays for AI systems; check its current status

blocks.title: Build your own
blocks.text: A bank group could define an overlay for all payment systems: supplement Moderate with stronger integrity controls (SI-7 enhancements), fixed parameter values, and extra supplier controls. Every payment system then starts from the same tailored set.

A system can have several overlays (e.g. cloud + privacy + OT). Where overlays conflict, the organisation resolves it with risk-based decisions and documents the outcome in the SSP. Overlays reduce effort but don't replace system-specific tailoring.

quiz.q: What is an overlay?
options: A reusable set of tailoring decisions for a community, technology or environment
quiz.explain: Overlays are shared tailoring.

quiz.q: Which NIST publication contains an overlay for operational technology?
quiz.explain: SP 800-82 Rev. 3 includes an OT overlay.

quiz.q: FedRAMP baselines are best described as...
options: Tailored SP 800-53 Rev. 5 baselines for cloud services
quiz.explain: They tailor SP 800-53 baselines with parameter values.

chapters.title: Applying baselines in practice
chapters.summary: FedRAMP, private-sector use, a worked tailoring case and common pitfalls.

items: **FedRAMP** authorises cloud services for US federal use. Its Rev. 5 baselines (Low, Moderate, High, and a tailored Low-impact SaaS option) start from SP 800-53B and add parameter values and extra requirements. FedRAMP has also been modernising its process (the "FedRAMP 20x" initiative); check its current status.
**CMMC and SP 800-171** protect controlled unclassified information in the US defence supply chain; SP 800-171 requirements derive from the Moderate baseline.
**StateRAMP** and similar programmes reuse the same baselines for state and local government.
Adopt the **Moderate baseline** as a corporate control library for important systems and **Low** for minor ones; add **High** selectively for crown jewels.
Map the tailored baseline to **CSF 2.0** subcategories for board reporting and to **ISO/IEC 27001** Annex A for certification.
Use **overlays** for recurring system types (cloud SaaS, payment systems, OT).
Keep parameter values in a central standard so every system uses the same numbers.

sections.title: Worked case: a SaaS HR platform

items: **Categorise:** employee records (C Moderate, I Moderate, A Low) and payroll data (C Moderate, I Moderate, A Moderate). High-water mark: **Moderate**.
**Select:** Moderate baseline (287 items) plus the Privacy baseline (96 items; many overlap) because the system processes PII.
**Common controls:** physical and environmental (PE) inherited from the SaaS provider's certified data centres; enterprise IAM (IA-2, AC-2 parts) inherited from the corporate identity provider.
**Scope:** AC-18 wireless not applicable to the SaaS backend; MA controls largely provider-owned.

**Compensate:** the provider doesn't allow customers to scan its infrastructure (RA-5), so the organisation relies on the provider's contractual scanning and remediation reports, and scans its own configurations and integrations.
**Parameters:** AC-7 = 5 attempts/15 minutes; AU-11 = 13 months; RA-5 = monthly scans.
**Supplement:** add SR-6 supplier assessments and AU-13 monitoring for information disclosure because of the sensitivity of payroll data.
**Document:** all decisions in the SSP; the authorising official reviews and grants the ATO.
Selecting a baseline without a documented categorisation.
Leaving parameters undefined, so controls can't be tested.
Scoping controls out without rationale, which auditors treat as gaps.
Forgetting the privacy baseline for systems that process PII.
Assuming a cloud provider covers controls that are actually shared or customer-owned.
Never revisiting tailoring when the system or threats change.

quiz.q: A SaaS HR system's C/I/A high-water mark is Moderate and it processes PII. What is selected?
quiz.explain: Moderate by categorisation; privacy because of PII.

quiz.q: SP 800-171 requirements for protecting CUI derive from which baseline?
quiz.explain: SP 800-171 is derived from the Moderate baseline.

quiz.q: What is a common pitfall in applying baselines?
quiz.explain: Undefined parameters make controls untestable.
